summary.text: 走 is an old graph interpreted in early forms as a running person, later associated with the action “run.” Its present standardized shape resembles 土 above 龰, but those modern-looking parts do not establish the graph’s original construction.

formation.text: Pictographic is the best-supported account of the oldest proposed construction: paleographic analysis reads the early graph as a person running with swinging arms. Some later bronze forms add 止, interpreted as emphasizing the feet. The received Shuowen account instead analyzes the seal-script form as 夭 plus 止 and explains 夭 as bending; that is evidence for a Han-era interpretation, not proof of the oldest graph’s parts. The two analyses should remain distinct.

history.text: The curated image is a modern digital rendering of the Shuowen seal-script form. It illustrates that received tradition, not the earliest graph; no direct oracle-bone glyph image is included, and the rendering was not visually inspected for this account.

Paleographic accounts describe oracle-bone, bronze, Warring States, seal, clerical, and regular-script records, with later forms increasingly altered. The upper running-person figure was interpreted as 夭 in the Shuowen tradition. The modern top 土 and bottom 龰 are descriptions of the standardized graph, not evidence that 土 was an ancient semantic component.

uncertainties.text: The earliest graph’s internal structure remains an interpretation. Accounts disagree over whether the early form is a running-person pictograph and whether 止 was added in later bronze forms; the received Shuowen decomposition belongs to a different historical analysis.

Oracle-bone examples are reported in place-name and personal-name contexts, so they do not independently establish the verb “run” there. A clear verbal example is reported in a Western Zhou bronze inscription, but exact inscription dating and a securely dated first occurrence are not supplied.

The cited dictionaries list senses including running, fleeing, going toward, and walking, but do not establish a complete dated path between them. No transition should be treated as certain from the order of modern glosses.

senses.text: Paleographic reporting identifies a clear bronze-inscription verb use in the phrase 夙夜奔走. Oracle-bone examples are reported as names or place-name contexts, so they do not establish an earlier verbal use.
Classical citations use 走 for fleeing or escaping. The supplied evidence does not securely date the individual textual witnesses or establish when this sense developed from “run.”
Dictionaries record uses meaning to go or tend toward, but the supplied examples do not establish their chronology relative to “run” or “flee.”

The modern character commonly means walking or going on foot. This differs from the classical “run” sense, but the evidence does not establish when or by what sequence the broader walking sense became current.

limitations.text: The evidence supports the verb “run” in Western Zhou bronze contexts but does not establish a securely dated first use. Oracle-bone examples cited here are not independently verbal attestations.
The senses of fleeing, going toward, and walking are documented, but their semantic connections and chronology remain unresolved in this dossier.

overview.text: The oldest proposed graph pictures a running person, and “run” is reported in Western Zhou bronze writing. Today 走 commonly means “walk” or “go on foot”; the precise path from the older running sense is not established here.
